misconceptions: Errors can be returned as 200 with an error field
An idempotent request must return the same response every time
no-cache means that a response must not be stored
ETags only help with caching, not with concurrent updates
Removing a field that looks unused is a non-breaking change

templates.question: What is the difference between PUT, PATCH and POST? Which HTTP methods are safe and which are idempotent, and why does it matter?
keyPoints: POST creates a resource in a collection or triggers processing, and is not idempotent
PUT replaces the resource at a known URI and is idempotent
PATCH applies a partial update and is not necessarily idempotent
Safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) do not change state
Idempotent methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE) have the same effect when repeated, so they can be retried safely

templates.question: Which status codes would you return for a successful create, a validation error, a missing resource, an unauthenticated request, a forbidden request and a conflicting update?
keyPoints: 201 Created with a Location header for a successful create
400 Bad Request (or 422) for invalid input
404 Not Found for a missing resource
401 Unauthorized when the client is not authenticated, 403 Forbidden when it is authenticated but not allowed
409 Conflict, or 412 Precondition Failed with If-Match, for a conflicting update; 5xx only for server faults

templates.question: Design the REST endpoints of a library system in which members borrow and return books. How do you model borrowing and returning?
keyPoints: Resources are nouns: /books, /members, /loans
Borrowing creates a loan: POST /loans with the book and the member
Returning updates the loan, for example PATCH /loans/{id} setting returnedAt
GET /members/{id}/loans lists a member's loans
Avoid verbs in URLs such as /borrowBook

templates.question: A client sometimes creates duplicate records when its POST request times out and its HTTP library retries automatically. What is the cause, and what are your options?
keyPoints: The first POST may have succeeded on the server although the client never received the response
POST is not idempotent, so the retry creates a second record
An idempotency key sent by the client and stored by the server makes the retry return the first result
Or let the client choose the id and use PUT, which is idempotent
Or enforce a unique natural key, and do not retry non-idempotent requests automatically

templates.question: How do Cache-Control, ETag and If-None-Match work together to cache GET responses?
keyPoints: Cache-Control says who may cache a response and for how long (max-age, private, public, no-store)
no-cache allows storing but requires revalidation before each use
The server sends an ETag identifying the version of the representation
The client revalidates with If-None-Match, and the server answers 304 Not Modified without a body when nothing changed

templates.question: Two users edit the same customer record and both press save; the second save silently overwrites the first. How would you prevent this with HTTP?
keyPoints: It is a lost update
Return an ETag (or a version) with GET
The client sends it back in If-Match with its PUT or PATCH
The server compares it with the current version and answers 412 Precondition Failed when it differs
On the server this maps to optimistic locking with a version column

templates.question: What is the difference between strong and weak ETags, and how would you generate ETags for resources stored in a database?
keyPoints: A strong ETag means byte-for-byte identical representations; a weak one (W/ prefix) means equivalent
Deriving it from a version column or the last-modified time is cheap
Hashing the representation works for anything, but the body must be built first
If-None-Match accepts weak comparison; If-Match for updates needs strong comparison

templates.question: After an update, some users keep seeing the old product price for several minutes while others already see the new one. What could cause it?
keyPoints: A cached response is served by a browser, CDN or proxy until its max-age expires
The response was marked cacheable for too long
Different users hit different caches or edge locations
Use a short max-age or no-cache with ETag revalidation for changing data, and purge the CDN on update

templates.question: What should a good REST error response contain? Describe the problem details format.
keyPoints: An accurate HTTP status
A machine-readable error type or code, a short title and a human-readable detail
Field-level errors for validation failures
RFC 9457 problem details (application/problem+json) standardise type, title, status, detail and instance, with extensions
A correlation id, and no internal details or stack traces

templates.question: Design the list endpoint of a transactions resource with filters on date range and status, sorting, and pagination over millions of rows.
keyPoints: GET /transactions with query parameters for the filters, the sort and a page size limit
Cursor (keyset) pagination with an opaque next cursor for large data, ordered by a unique key
A maximum page size
The response includes the next cursor or link
The filter and sort columns are indexed, and the parameters are validated

templates.question: How do you evolve a REST API without breaking existing clients, and when do you need a new version?
keyPoints: Additive changes are compatible: new optional fields and new endpoints
Clients must ignore fields they do not know (tolerant reader)
Removing or renaming fields, or changing their types or meaning, breaks clients and needs a new version (URL, header or media type)
Deprecate with notice and a sunset date, and run the versions side by side
Compare OpenAPI contracts or run contract tests in CI

templates.question: After a backend release, a client breaks because a numeric id is now returned as a string, although no field was removed. How should this have been caught, and how should the change have been made?
keyPoints: Changing a field's type is a breaking change
A published contract (OpenAPI) compared in CI detects it
Consumer-driven contract tests (for example Pact) check what clients actually rely on
Add a new field or a new version instead of changing the type in place
